title: Hume and Smith
keyWorks: D. Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (1739–1740)
D. Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748)
A. Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759)
summary: Hume and Smith were friends and the leading figures of the eighteenth-century Scottish Enlightenment. They studied human beings as part of nature, relying on observation, and concluded that our lives are governed far more by feelings and habits than by pure reason — and that morality grows out of people's capacity to respond to one another's feelings.
onEmotions: Hume held that it is feelings (the “passions”) that set our goals, while reason only helps us find the way to them: he famously called reason the “slave of the passions.” He distinguished violent passions from calm ones and showed how feelings pass from person to person through “sympathy” — our capacity to catch another's state. Adam Smith developed this idea: we constantly imagine ourselves in other people's place and see ourselves through their eyes. This is how the “impartial spectator” forms in us — an inner fair and kindly gaze that helps us bring our feelings into proportion without suppressing them.

anxiety.text: “Be a philosopher; but, amidst all your philosophy, be still a man,” Hume advised. Anxiety is a very human response to uncertainty, and the Scots explained it without reproach. Hume wrote that hope and fear are born of uncertainty: when the imagination wavers between a good outcome and a bad one, the mind swings between joy and sorrow, and out of these mixed feelings comes unease. This means anxiety is not an error in thinking but the work of an imagination that honestly sees several possibilities. Hume also distinguished “violent” from “calm” passions: the calm ones are less noticeable, yet sometimes they shape our actions more strongly. So you needn't try to chase away a stormy anxiety; instead, you can notice the quiet, steady feelings and values beside it — they are in you too, and they also shape your life.
anxiety.practice: A Humean tuning: put a hand on your chest and, beneath the loud anxiety, look for a quiet, “calm passion” — attachment to someone, the wish to live honestly. Name it out loud and stay with it for three breaths.

fear.text: A man hangs over a precipice in a sturdy iron cage and trembles, though he knows perfectly well he won't fall — Hume drew this picture to show that fear needn't obey arguments. Imagination and habit are stronger than abstract knowledge. Hume showed that feelings are not derived from reasoning and cannot be removed by it directly. This frees you from the needless reproach of “but I know there's nothing to be afraid of.” You can know — and still be afraid; that is how human beings are made. Adam Smith added that courage is not the absence of fear but “self-command”: the ability, while feeling fear, to act in due proportion anyway, leaning on a calm inner spectator.
fear.practice: Picture a calm, kindly person watching you from the side, like Smith's impartial spectator. What would they suggest you do in the next five minutes?

sadness.text: When we tell a friend about our sorrow, we seem to live it again — and yet it grows lighter: Adam Smith examines this paradox at the very start of his book on moral sentiments. Sadness is a legitimate feeling, and what interested him most was how to carry it. Another person's sympathy softens the pain, because we begin to see our trouble partly through their eyes, a little more calmly. Hume called this capacity “sympathy”: feelings naturally pass from one person to another. The conclusion is simple: sadness doesn't have to be borne alone and in silence. Sharing it doesn't mean burdening others; it means letting an ancient, natural mechanism of consolation do its work — the very mechanism on which, in the Scots' view, all of human life rests.
sadness.practice: Say one sentence about your sadness to someone — out loud, on the phone or in a voice message — and let them simply sympathize, without advice. Smith would call this mutual sympathy.

grief.text: “Time, the great and universal comforter,” Adam Smith wrote — and yet he demanded no haste from the grieving. He described with great subtlety what happens to grief among other people. Those around us, he wrote, cannot feel our loss as sharply as we do; so in their company we involuntarily soften the expression of our pain a little, and this makes us a little calmer ourselves. Alone, we feel grief in full force. Both states are natural: the need to cry it out alone and the relief of having others near. Smith also believed that especially deep sorrow stirs profound sympathy in people. Grief doesn't have to be “proportionate” to anyone's expectations. It simply needs time and, where possible, people nearby.
grief.practice: Ask what the grief is asking for right now — solitude or someone's presence — and give it that without excuses: close the door, or ask someone to sit beside you in silence.

loneliness.text: A person raised in complete solitude, Smith wrote, could no more think of his own character than of the beauty of his own face — he would have no mirror. Loneliness hurts because we are deeply social creatures. Hume wrote that complete solitude is perhaps the greatest hardship a person can suffer, since almost all our passions come alive only in connection with others. According to Smith, we constantly need “mutual sympathy” — someone to share our feelings. Without it, joy fades and sorrow grows heavier. This is not a whim; it is human nature itself, as described by sober observers. Such a view lifts the shame from loneliness: you are simply missing something all people need. And it reminds you that even a small act of shared feeling matters.
loneliness.practice: Find yourself Smith's “mirror” for today: one short live encounter — a chat with a neighbor, a call, a few words with a shop assistant. Notice what comes alive in you when a feeling is shared.

quote.text: Nothing pleases us more than to observe in other men a fellow-feeling with all the emotions of our own breast.
quote.author: Adam Smith
quote.source: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part I, Sec. I, Ch. 2

anger.text: “A person becomes contemptible who tamely sits still, and submits to insults,” wrote Smith, a moralist hardly fond of quarrels. For him anger is a natural feeling with an important role. He called it “resentment” and believed nature gave it to us for protection: it guards justice and keeps us from being wronged with impunity. At the same time, Smith noted that anger belongs to the “unsocial” passions — others find it hard to share until they understand what happened. So he suggested looking at the situation through the eyes of the “impartial spectator” — someone who knows everything but has no stake in anyone's winning. If that spectator would agree you were wronged, your resentment is legitimate. This view helps you not to renounce your anger but to find its fair measure.
anger.practice: Hold a one-minute Smithian court: picture an impartial witness who saw the whole scene. Ask them: what response would be proportionate — no more and no less than the offence?

shame.text: Hume set two passions side by side — pride and “humility,” that is, shame: both look at our self and largely reflect others' opinions, as in a mirror. Right now the mirror is showing you something unpleasant, and that hurts. Adam Smith added an important refinement: we want not only approval but also to be worthy of it. So shame before the crowd and shame before the inner impartial spectator are different things. The first can be unjust; the second is more honest and more kind. Ask yourself: would a fair and kindly person who knew all the circumstances condemn me? Often the answer turns out gentler than the voice of shame.
shame.practice: Move the shame from “the crowd” to “the man within the breast”: picture a witness who knows every circumstance and wishes you well, and ask what one word they would use for what you're ashamed of.

quote.text: Man naturally desires, not only to be loved, but to be lovely.
quote.author: Adam Smith
quote.source: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part III, Ch. 2

guilt.text: “The man within the breast, the great judge and arbiter of our conduct” — that is what Adam Smith called the inner impartial spectator, and it seems to be speaking in you now. Guilt shows that doing right matters to you, and Smith deeply respected this feeling. But Smith also noticed an important subtlety: we often feel guilty even for what happened by accident, without any ill intent — simply because we turned out to be the cause of someone else's misfortune. He considered this feeling natural and noble in its own way, but stressed that a fair spectator judges above all by intentions, not by chance outcomes. So guilt is worth checking: what here truly depended on my will, and what on circumstances? This question doesn't remove responsibility, but it makes it honest.
guilt.practice: A Smithian sorting on your palms: in your right hand, mentally place what depended on your intentions and decisions; in your left, chance and circumstance. Hold both and feel which is heavier.

envy.text: A common soldier envies not the general but his sergeant, and a writer envies not a philosopher but another writer: this is how Hume showed that envy is aroused not by vast difference but by closeness. We judge things not in themselves but by comparison, and the same good seems great or small depending on what we set it against. If envy is stinging you now, this is worth remembering. This observation helps you see that envy is the work of a “comparing” imagination, not an objective assessment of your life. You can notice it without shame and ask: whom am I comparing myself to right now, and why?
envy.practice: Change the point of comparison, as Hume might suggest: set beside yourself not the “sergeant” but yourself a year ago. Spend a minute recalling what has changed, grown or got easier since then.

emptiness.text: In the spring of 1734 the young Hume wrote a long letter to a physician: after months of intense study his former ardour had died away, his thoughts had grown cold, and it was hard for him to do anything. He knew emptiness and apathy from the inside. What helped him, by his own account, was not effort of will but a gradual return to a regular life, to movement and to the company of people. This fits his philosophy: reason by itself cannot make us want anything; desire and motion are born of feelings. Apathy, then, is not a failure of will or “laziness” but a temporary dimming of the passions. They can't be switched back on by command, but you can create conditions in which they slowly come back to life.
emptiness.practice: Hume's own prescription: walk for ten minutes at a steady pace — around the yard or the room will do — expecting no feelings from yourself. For Hume, motion sometimes comes before desire.

quote.text: Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions, and can never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.
quote.author: David Hume
quote.source: A Treatise of Human Nature, Book II, Part 3, Sec. 3

confusion.text: A sailor who has barely escaped shipwreck puts out to sea again in the same leaky, weather-beaten boat — that is how Hume saw himself at the end of the first book of the Treatise. Even the greatest minds know confusion. There he also described it: having pushed his doubts to the limit, he felt lost, surrounded on every side by questions without answers. The way out, he admitted, came not from a new theory. He dined, played a game of backgammon, talked and laughed with his friends — and after a few hours his tormenting doubts seemed far away. Hume didn't consider this an escape: nature itself brings us back to life, and we can return to hard questions later, with fresh strength. Your confusion doesn't demand an immediate solution. Sometimes the best thing you can do is give yourself a break in simple human things.
confusion.practice: Do as Hume did: set the question aside for the evening and play something — cards, a board game, even noughts and crosses with someone nearby. Then look at the question again.

quote.text: Be a philosopher; but, amidst all your philosophy, be still a man.
quote.author: David Hume
quote.source: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. I

fatigue.text: “The poor man's son, whom heaven in its anger has visited with ambition” — so Adam Smith begins one of his bitterest parables. Your tiredness is real, and the parable is about it. From childhood this young man is drawn to wealth and recognition. All his life he toils without rest, sacrificing a tranquillity that was within his reach from the very start — and only near the end does he realize that much of what he chased was worth less than the peace he lost. Smith doesn't condemn the pursuit of a better life; he simply notes that happiness depends on tranquillity more than we think. Your fatigue, then, is an honest voice reminding you of rest. Rest is not lost time but a return to that without which joy is impossible.
fatigue.practice: Give yourself what Smith's poor man's son put off all his life: fifteen minutes of tranquillity right now — lie down, close your eyes, achieve nothing.

quote.text: Happiness consists in tranquillity and enjoyment. Without tranquillity there can be no enjoyment.
quote.author: Adam Smith
quote.source: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part III, Ch. 3

boredom.text: A card game without stakes is dull, Hume observed — not out of greed, but because the mind has nothing to enliven it. Boredom is natural, and he explained it through the way the human mind works. For Hume, the mind is drawn to lively impressions: to anything that enlivens it and sets it in motion — a game, a conversation, a new task, or even someone else's story. When such impressions are absent, the mind grows sluggish, and this is felt as boredom. So boredom is not a sign that something is wrong with you but a sign of the mind's hunger for liveliness. Hume also stressed the role of company: people's feelings pass to one another through “sympathy,” and around others even ordinary things grow brighter. You can take boredom as a signal: you're missing living contact with the world.
boredom.practice: Give your mind a small “stake”: set yourself a playful five-minute task — find seven blue things in the room, guess how many steps it is to the window, then check.

joy.text: “How selfish soever man may be supposed, there are evidently some principles in his nature which interest him in the fortune of others” — so opens Adam Smith's book on moral sentiments. That is why joy asks to be shared. Hume showed that through “sympathy” feelings pass from person to person and grow stronger as they do: joy seen in another enlivens us too. So shared joy is not diminished but grows. Your joy is not only your private affair; in Hume's and Smith's view, it naturally spreads to those around you and makes life together warmer. Allow yourself to feel it fully — and, if you like, share it with someone.
joy.practice: Share the joy with one person — call them or tell them in person — and notice how, as Hume said, it comes back to you stronger, reflected in their face.

quote.text: How selfish soever man may be supposed, there are evidently some principles in his nature, which interest him in the fortune of others, and render their happiness necessary to him, though he derives nothing from it except the pleasure of seeing it.
quote.author: Adam Smith
quote.source: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part I, Sec. I, Ch. 1

love.text: In the Paris salons Hume was fondly called “le bon David,” good David, and he knew how to be a tender friend. He considered love and tenderness among the most natural human feelings. Hume described love as a passion directed at another person and aroused by their qualities — kindness, intelligence, beauty, closeness to us. He showed how love is born of proximity, habit and sympathy, that is, how it grows out of the very fabric of shared life. Adam Smith added that tenderness, kindness and affection are “social” feelings: people find it easy and pleasant to share them, so they warm not only the one who loves and the one who is loved but everyone around. So tenderness needn't be hidden or felt as shameful: it is one of the feelings that hold human society together.
love.practice: Do one small “social” act, as Smith would put it: tell this person which of their qualities most stirs your tenderness.

gratitude.text: “The never to be forgotten Dr Hutcheson” — so Adam Smith, almost half a century later, spoke of his university teacher. Gratitude is a warm and natural feeling, and Smith knew it from the inside. Adam Smith described it as a passion that directly prompts us to return good to the one who has done us good. He saw it as the opposite of resentment: just as resentment guards justice, gratitude sustains goodwill between people. Smith noted that it matters to us not only to repay a benefactor but also that they know their kindness was noticed. Hume, for his part, saw gratitude as an expression of sympathy: we respond to the care we have felt. Gratitude, then, is not a duty but one of the natural ways people bind themselves to one another. You can simply live it — and, if you wish, express it.
gratitude.practice: Do what Smith thought mattered: let your benefactor know their kindness was noticed — in one sentence, by message or in person, even if many years have passed.

hope.text: How do we know the sun will rise tomorrow? Hume asked, and answered honestly: only from custom and experience. Hope lives on the same ground, and he described its mechanics very precisely. He wrote that hope arises when the imagination, wavering between different outcomes, leans toward the good one. There is always a share of uncertainty in it — which is why it lives next door to fear. But that doesn't make hope naive: for Hume, all our expectations rest on habit and experience rather than absolute certainty, and that is how all people live. So you can calmly accept that your hope isn't guaranteed — such is the nature of any look into the future. And yet it already shapes your life now: it gives you strength and colours the day. You can cherish it without demanding promises from it.
hope.practice: At sunset or tomorrow morning, look at the sun as a Humean argument: it guarantees nothing, yet it keeps coming back. Recall one time something good happened despite your uncertainty.

nostalgia.text: After long years in London and Paris, Hume returned to his native Edinburgh — to old friends, familiar streets and suppers. Nostalgia is a tender, slightly sad feeling, and he helps us understand how it arises. He described the laws of the “association of ideas”: one thought calls up another through resemblance, contiguity in time or place, or cause and effect. That is why a smell, a tune or a street can suddenly carry us into the past. Hume also noted that memories are only “fainter copies” of vivid impressions: they resemble the past but lack its full brightness. Hence the particular softness and sadness of nostalgia: we reach for what we remember but cannot live through again. There is nothing wrong in this. Nostalgia shows which impressions left a deep mark on you — that is, what is truly dear to you.
nostalgia.practice: Follow a Humean chain of associations live: play a tune or find a scent from that time and for a minute simply watch which memory arrives first, and then which feeling follows.

craving.text: Hume built a theory of government on one human weakness: we prefer the near good to the distant one. He would explain a sharp “I want it right now” without reproach. He noticed a pattern everyone can confirm: what is near in time and space acts on our passions far more strongly than what is distant. That is why people so often prefer a small good now to a greater good later . It isn't stupidity; it's how the imagination works. Hume also distinguished “violent” from “calm” passions and called the ability of the calm passions to prevail over the violent ones over time “strength of mind.” A craving is a violent passion: it rises like a wave and, unfed, subsides. Beneath it live your calm, long-term desires — and you can give them a little time so their voice becomes easier to hear.
craving.practice: Call on a “calm passion”: while the wave of craving rises and falls, breathe slowly and hold one long-term wish in mind — health, a relationship, a clear head in the morning. The wave will pass; the wish will stay.

addiction.text: “Custom is the great guide of human life,” Hume wrote, and he described subtly how it works. In his language, addiction is not a moral failure but the force of habit that operates in every person. Repetition, he wrote, gradually weakens the pleasure we take in something, yet at the same time strengthens our inclination toward it: doing it becomes easier, and giving it up harder. Many who know addiction from the inside will recognize themselves here: less and less joy, and an ever tighter circle. Hume saw no vice in this — only a mechanism of nature. But in his essay “The Sceptic” he also observed the reverse: habit is one of the most powerful means of gradually changing one's mind and inclinations. What was built by repetition can be rebuilt by repetition.
addiction.practice: If custom is the guide, give it a new route: choose a tiny action — a glass of water, three squats, a step onto the balcony — and repeat it at the hour the craving usually comes. And if you like, find a mutual-help group where people walk this path together.

quote.text: Custom, then, is the great guide of human life.
quote.author: David Hume
quote.source: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. V, Part I

hangover.text: “Who can tell me what his thoughts were on the first of January 1715, or the eleventh of March 1719?” Hume asked, reflecting on what the “self” is. On the morning after drinking, when body and soul both feel heavy and memory has gaps, this odd question offers unexpected support. And does it follow from our having forgotten it that it wasn't I back then? Our identity, for Hume, rests not on an unbroken memory but on the connection of impressions — everyone's memory has gaps. Adam Smith would add: judge yesterday not with the voice of morning panic but through the eyes of an impartial spectator who knows all the circumstances and wishes you well. That spectator will most likely be gentler than your thoughts this morning.
hangover.practice: Postpone the trial of yesterday: for now, a glass of water, a little food and rest. In a few hours, if needed, look back at yesterday through the eyes of a kindly witness.

euphoria.text: Hume valued a turn of mind that sees the bright side of things more than being born to an estate of ten thousand a year. He certainly wouldn't want to spoil a vivid burst of euphoria. Hume considered liveliness of impressions one of the mind's chief pleasures: whatever enlivens us is pleasant in itself. He noticed that novelty and surprise especially intensify any passion: a sudden good seems greater than a familiar one. This idea doesn't devalue your high; it explains its brightness. Adam Smith added that people find it easiest to share small joys, while very great and sudden delight is something others can't always take up at once — which is why euphoria can sometimes feel lonely. You can fully enjoy this state without demanding that others share it with the same intensity.
euphoria.practice: Split the high Hume's way into two parts: what comes from novelty and what comes from something you truly hold dear. Keep the second — as a note on your phone or a word said to someone close.

crash.text: Smith collected stories of people who fell sharply from a height — from deposed kings to ruined rich men. A drop after a high is hard, but in these stories Smith found a pattern that may offer a little comfort. He observed that every person's mind sooner or later returns to its usual, natural state of tranquillity: after good fortune it sinks back to it in time, after misfortune it rises back up. The crash is part of the same movement: after a high wave the mind returns to its level, and in the moment of return this feels like falling. Hume would explain the sharpness too: we judge our state by comparison, and an ordinary day next to a celebration seems dull. But that also means the greyness is partly created by contrast. It will pass, just as the high did.
crash.practice: Do one simple, habitual thing that usually steadies you — make tea, make the bed, walk around the block — and tell yourself in Smith's spirit: “I'm not falling; I'm returning to my level.”

quote.text: The mind of every man, in a longer or shorter time, returns to its natural and usual state of tranquillity. In prosperity, after a certain time, it falls back to that state; in adversity, after a certain time, it rises up to it.
quote.author: Adam Smith
quote.source: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part III, Ch. 3

panic.text: “The mind is a kind of theatre, where several perceptions successively make their appearance; pass, re-pass, glide away,” Hume wrote. When a wave of panic hits, terror seizes the body and thoughts race — on that stage everything moves especially fast. Nothing in this flow stays the same — terror included. Even the most violent passions, for Hume, do not stand still: they rise and weaken. Usually such a wave peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Adam Smith called “self-command” not the absence of fear but the ability to live through it without letting it decide for you. Right now you don't need to decide anything or convince yourself of anything — it is enough to lean on your body and let the wave pass.
panic.practice: Take a seat in Hume's theatre: press your feet into the floor, breathe out more slowly than you breathe in, and silently name five things you see and three sounds you hear — like a spectator watching the scene change.

dread.text: Why should tomorrow resemble yesterday? What links cause and effect? Hume's questions make the head spin. The question “what's the point of it all” comes to thinking people, and he knew its taste. At the end of the first book of the Treatise he described how, having pushed his questions to the limit, he felt like a strange, solitary creature amid darkness. In another work he confessed that the world as a whole is a riddle, an enigma the human mind cannot solve. Hume didn't pretend to know the answer. But he noticed that nature itself brings us back to life: to people, conversation, everyday tasks — and in them meaning is felt, even if it can't be proved. Adam Smith would add that human beings are made for connection with others and find support in it. The question “why” can stay open while you live.
dread.practice: Let ordinary life bring you back, as nature brought Hume back: cook a simple meal or go out among people — to a shop, the yard — and exchange a few words with someone.

fomo.text: King Pyrrhus was listing his future conquests — Italy, Sicily, Carthage — and after each one his counsellor Cineas asked: “And then?” Adam Smith retold the story for everyone who feels that real life is happening somewhere without them. “Then,” the king replied, “we shall live at ease and rejoice with our friends.” “And what keeps you from doing that now?” the counsellor asked. Smith saw a common trap here: we often chase what is already within reach, only in another form. He also noted that much of what we desire we want not for the pleasure of it but to be looked at and noticed. The fear of missing out may be that desire for attention. Ask yourself: what do I actually want — and isn't it already close at hand?
fomo.practice: Ask yourself Cineas's question — “What keeps me from doing this now?” — and do a small version today of what you fear missing: meeting a friend, a walk, an evening with music.

sleepless.text: At night, for Hume, the copies start competing with the originals: pale “ideas” grow almost as vivid as living “impressions.” Racing thoughts at three in the morning are agonizing, and he helps explain why everything seems more frightening at night. He distinguished “impressions” — the vivid sensations we receive from the world — from “ideas,” their paler copies. Usually impressions are brighter than ideas. But Hume noted that in sleep, in a fever or in great agitation, ideas can come close to impressions in force. At night, when there are few impressions and the body is tired, thoughts and imagined pictures become almost as vivid as reality. This doesn't mean you see the truth more clearly at night — if anything, the opposite. In the morning, in daylight and among people, these same thoughts usually seem much smaller.
sleepless.practice: Give your body one living Humean “impression” in place of ideas: touch the fabric of the blanket, feel the pillow's coolness on your cheek, listen to your breathing. Whisper: “This is night-time vividness, not the real scale.”

betrayal.text: Hume helped Rousseau move to England and sought a royal pension for him — and Rousseau suddenly declared him part of a plot against him. Betrayal wounds deeply, and Hume knew it not only from books. Hume showed that all of human life together rests on trust and promises: we can cooperate and be friends only if we rely on each other's word. So betrayal is a blow not only to a relationship but to the very ground on which we stand beside others. Adam Smith considered resentment at injustice natural and legitimate if an impartial spectator who knew the circumstances would share it. Such a spectator would most likely understand you. Your pain is not excessive — it is proportionate to how much the trust mattered. And the ability to trust again will return when you find people who deserve it.
betrayal.practice: Take a walk and, as you go, tell the whole story to Smith's imagined impartial spectator — under your breath, as if to a friend. At the end, ask: would they share my resentment?

jealousy.text: “Though a lover may be good company to his mistress, he is so to nobody else,” Smith teased. Jealousy is different: its fears anyone understands, and it truly hurts. Hume showed that we judge everything by comparison: the same thing seems great or small depending on what stands beside it. In jealousy, the imagination places us beside a rival and starts comparing — usually not in our favour. Adam Smith observed that love itself often seems incomprehensible to outsiders, yet the anxieties and fears of loss that accompany it anyone understands at once. So your jealousy is a very human feeling, not something shameful. But it helps to remember: the pictures painted by the comparing imagination are not facts. Ask what you actually know, and what has been filled in by fear.
jealousy.practice: Separate what you know from what you imagine, and pick one thing you could calmly ask the person close to you. Ask it — gently, without accusation — and listen to the answer.

resentment.text: “The greatest poison to the happiness of a good mind” — so Adam Smith called hatred and resentment, yet he understood where they come from: you really were hurt. Adam Smith recognized resentment as a natural defence of justice. But he noticed something else as well: malice and resentment belong to the “unsocial” passions — they are unpleasant above all to the one who carries them, like something cutting inside. Hume would add: ideas fade over time unless they are revived, and each new replay of the old scene makes it vivid again. A grudge lives so long partly because memory keeps refreshing it. This is no reproach: that's how the imagination works. But it is also a hope — if you gradually return to the scene less often, the feeling may slowly weaken.
resentment.practice: Hume would say an idea fades unless it is revived. Today, simply count — on your fingers or on beads — how many times you mentally return to the scene of the hurt, without stopping yourself.

heartbreak.text: “The chief part of human happiness arises from the consciousness of being beloved,” Adam Smith wrote. That is why a broken heart hurts so much, and he explained why this pain is so hard to share. He observed that love is one of those passions others find hard to feel with the same force: from the outside, attachment to one particular person can seem out of proportion. So when people say “just forget it, you'll find someone else,” it hurts twice over. But Smith saw something else too: grief and loss are things others understand well, and their sympathy softens the pain. Hume would add that everything around you — places, things, songs — reminds you of the person who is gone, by the laws of association. This isn't your weakness; it's the work of memory. What you need is time, and people who understand what you've lost.
heartbreak.practice: Find one person who can listen without advice and ask, in Smith's spirit, for pure sympathy: “Right now I just need you to listen.”

impostor.text: Smith distinguished two desires: to be praised, and to be praiseworthy. The fear that any moment now they'll see through you says a surprising amount about the second. Impostor syndrome is precisely the voice of the second desire: you fear you're receiving recognition you haven't earned — which means that deserving it matters to you. That alone says a lot about you. Hume, for his part, knew self-doubt firsthand: his main work, A Treatise of Human Nature, in his own words “fell dead-born from the press.” That didn't stop him from becoming one of the greatest philosophers. Your doubts don't prove you don't belong — they show how seriously you take your work.
impostor.practice: Ask a colleague or friend who knows your work to name one thing you do well — and listen without arguing. This is the voice of “the man without,” worth checking against the one within.

self_hatred.text: So absent-minded was Adam Smith that he once fell into a tanning pit mid-conversation — yet history remembers him as a great thinker, not a klutz. Self-hatred is a heavy feeling, and the inner critic can sound like conscience. But Adam Smith drew an important distinction. The inner “impartial spectator,” for Smith, is fair and kindly: it knows all the circumstances and judges in proportion. Yet Smith acknowledged that its voice can be drowned out — by the noise of others' opinions, by humiliations you've lived through, by your own fears. A critic who only hates is not the spectator but a distortion. Hume went further still: he considered healthy self-respect a merit, and regarded self-abasement and mortification not as virtues but as things that only sour the temper and harden the heart. Neither of them would agree with the verdict this voice passes on you.
self_hatred.practice: Say one line from your inner critic out loud — then say the same thought in the voice of Smith's spectator, fair and kindly. How did the words change?

helplessness.text: Ten pin-factory workers, each doing one small step, make tens of thousands of pins a day — no one does everything. Helplessness is heaviest when a problem is huge and you're alone; Smith offered a relieving observation. The care of the happiness of the whole world, he wrote, is not the business of any single person; each of us is allotted a much humbler department — care for our own well-being, our family, our friends, our country. This is not a call to indifference. It is a recognition that human beings are made for a small circle, and within that circle their actions truly mean something. Hume would add that reason by itself doesn't move us — feelings do; so powerlessness can't be fixed by a single argument, but you can do one small thing that brings back a sense of your own strength.
helplessness.practice: Make your own “pin”: one small act in your near circle — help a neighbor, call a relative, tidy one corner. Not everything — just your operation.

procrastination.text: “Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions” — Hume's most daring line, and it explains a lot when you just can't get started. He showed that reason by itself cannot move us to act: it is always some feeling that moves us — desire, interest, curiosity. That is why arguments like “I have to, it's important” are so often powerless. Hume also reflected on how interest is born: in hunting or in a game, he wrote, the pleasure comes from the very activity of the mind, from the strain of attention — and the goal grows more important as you go. In other words, interest often appears not before you start but during. This frees you from having to “want to” first. You can begin with something small — and let the feeling catch up with you along the way.
procrastination.practice: Hume said the interest in hunting comes in the course of the chase. Start a five-minute “hunt”: set a timer and work on the task, promising yourself nothing beyond that.

uprooted.text: Hume, like many Scots of his day, felt something of an outsider in London and even compiled a list of “Scotticisms” — expressions that gave away his origins — to weed out of his books. Being cut off from home is a deep experience, and he knew what it is to be a stranger. He lived for long periods in France; he wrote his main book in the small town of La Flèche. Hume also noticed that people who live side by side gradually take on one another's manners and feelings through “sympathy” — the natural contagiousness of feeling. This means that in a new place you aren't doomed to estrangement: connections and habits grow gradually, through simple everyday contact. Homesickness is legitimate — and alongside it, something new is already growing.
uprooted.practice: Take a Humean walk in your new place: go along the same short route and notice one thing that has already become familiar — a sign, a tree, someone's face. For Hume, fellow-feeling grows with nearness and repetition.

overload.text: Imagine, Adam Smith proposed, that the great empire of China were swallowed up by an earthquake, and a man in Europe hears of it: he sincerely sympathizes — then returns to his business and sleeps soundly. An endless feed acts as if all such news should reach us at once — no wonder the overload feels like a real strain. Yet a small misfortune in his own life would rob him of sleep. Smith didn't condemn this; he described it: our capacity for fellow-feeling is built for the near circle. Today the feed pours hundreds of other people's troubles and events onto us every day — more than a human heart can hold. Your exhaustion is not callousness or weakness but a natural limit. Protecting your attention means preserving your ability to care.
overload.practice: Close the feed and keep, in Smith's sense, a “near circle”: one piece of news or one question that truly concerns you and those close to you. Think only about it for a minute; the rest can wait.

unreality.text: “When I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other, of heat or cold, light or shade, love or hatred,” Hume admitted. If it feels as though everything around you, or you yourself, is not quite real, that is frightening — but his discovery can make it less so. He found no separate “self” behind them. For Hume this didn't mean there was no self: it's just that the “self” is a living stream of impressions, not a solid object. Hume admitted that such reflections could plunge him into a cold bewilderment, but he noticed that nature itself brings us back to life — through ordinary tasks and the company of people. You are there, where the warmth, the light and the feeling are.
unreality.practice: Repeat Hume's experiment in reverse: catch one perception right now — warmth in your palms, light from the window, a sound — and name it out loud. That is you, here.

quote.text: For my part, when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other, of heat or cold, light or shade, love or hatred, pain or pleasure.
quote.author: David Hume
quote.source: A Treatise of Human Nature, Book I, Part 4, Sec. 6

awe.text: Before he died, Adam Smith had nearly all his drafts burned but spared an essay on the history of astronomy — on how wonder leads to knowledge. The Scots valued awe before the vast and the beautiful. Hume noticed that anything very large — a wide plain, the ocean, a long succession of ages — stirs a special admiration in us: the mind seems to expand as it tries to take in the object, and this expansion is pleasant in itself. Smith devoted that essay to wonder and admiration and believed that it was these that led people to philosophy and science: struck by something unusual, a person seeks a way to understand it. Awe, for Smith, is not childish naivety but the beginning of knowledge. Let it be, without rushing to explain it. Smith would probably say that you are now experiencing the very thing with which all of science once began.
awe.practice: Look at something vast — the sky, a river, an old tree — and let your mind, as Hume put it, “expand” as it tries to take it all in. For a minute, explain nothing.

relief.text: “What can be added to the happiness of the man who is in health, who is out of debt, and has a clear conscience?” Adam Smith asked. Relief is a warm and well-earned feeling, and the Scots help us savour it. Adam Smith observed that pain is almost always felt more sharply than the opposite pleasure. So when pain or anxiety leaves, the return to your ordinary state is experienced as real joy. Hume would explain this by the law of comparison: we judge our situation by setting it against what came before, and an ordinary calm day after strain seems bright. Relief is the moment when comparison works in your favour. Don't rush straight on to the next worry. And if you like, share your relief with someone: for Smith and Hume, shared joy grows stronger.
relief.practice: Say out loud: “It's over, and I feel lighter” — and share the news with someone who knew about your worry. Smith would say shared relief becomes fuller.

calm.text: For Hume, quiet inside is itself a feeling, not merely the absence of feelings. Where others saw cool reason, he saw “calm passions”: they don't rage, they are barely felt, and so they're easily mistaken for reason. But it is they — love of life, benevolence, attachment to what matters — that often guide us more strongly than the violent ones. Adam Smith saw happiness above all in tranquillity and enjoyment. Hume himself, describing his character, said he was a man of mild disposition, of command of temper, of an open, social and cheerful humour. Your calm is not a pause or an emptiness but a quiet strength that is in you. You can simply notice it.
calm.practice: Sit in this calm for two minutes doing nothing, and listen for which “calm passion” lives inside it: trust, gratitude, lightness. Name it in one word.

inspiration.text: “A new scene of thought” — that is how the eighteen-year-old Hume, in a letter, described the world of ideas that opened before him and into which he threw himself with ardour. He knew the joyful surge when thoughts fall into place by themselves. Then, from overwork, came a long slump — and Hume drew a lesson from it: he went back to work, alternating it with walks, exercise and company. His major works grew out of that inspiration. His experience says: inspiration is a real force, and it's worth trusting. But taking care of it means not burning yourself out in the first rush, and giving it a foothold in a steady life. Allow yourself this surge, and find a rhythm for it.
inspiration.practice: Write down the main idea and one first step — and next to it, following Hume's lesson, the time of your next walk or rest, so the surge lasts instead of burning you out.

schadenfreude.text: Hume titled a section of his Treatise, without any embarrassment, “Of malice and envy” — he didn't pretend these feelings were rare. Schadenfreude is an unpleasant discovery, but almost everyone has made it at least once. He explained it through the “principle of comparison”: we judge our situation not in itself but against others, and someone else's failure makes our own well-being seem brighter for a moment. That is, schadenfreude is not proof that you are corrupt but a side effect of the way the imagination constantly compares. Hume noticed something else too: sympathy — the capacity to catch another's feeling — is usually stronger in us. So schadenfreude rarely lasts long. You can simply notice it, without putting yourself on trial, and ask: which of my wounds did this other person's failure soothe for a second?
schadenfreude.practice: Test Humean sympathy: picture for a minute this person's face at the moment of failure — not an image, a living face. Notice whether something else stirs beside the schadenfreude.

contempt.text: Hume took apart, in the Treatise section “Of respect and contempt,” a feeling that is awkward to admit even to yourself — and found it is not simple at all. Contempt can still answer someone else's cruelty, falseness or foolishness. It contains a little dislike of the other and a little pride in oneself — since we compare and come out “above.” So contempt often props up our own dignity when it has been wounded somehow. Smith would add the question of the impartial spectator — an imagined fair witness who knows all the circumstances: what would they see in this person as a whole? This doesn't require you to give up your judgment. It helps you understand what in your contempt is a judgment about an action, and what is self-protection.
contempt.practice: Do Hume's analysis of the mixture: in your mind, separate “dislike of the act” from “pride in myself.” Which ingredient is bigger — and what in me was hurt?

disgust.text: Sancho Panza's kinsmen taste wine: one detects leather, the other iron, and everyone laughs — until a key on a leather thong turns up in the barrel. Hume retold this to show taste can be sharper than it seems; disgust is a kind of taste too. Hume believed our moral judgments are born not of cold reasoning but of feelings of approval and disapproval — rather like taste. Vice, he wrote, we find not in the action itself but in the feeling that rises in us when we look at it. Disgust, then, is not a mistake but information: it tells you that something important to you has been violated. But taste can be educated, and Smith suggested checking the feeling against the impartial spectator . If it's aimed at yourself, this witness is usually much gentler: they see not something “vile” but a person in hard circumstances who deserves understanding.
disgust.practice: In one sentence, name the value that the thing you're disgusted by violates. Then ask: how would a calm, kindly witness describe this situation?

revenge.text: A quiet Glasgow professor, Adam Smith wrote some of the most precise pages on vengeance in the history of ethics. If you want revenge, the injury was most likely real, and Smith would take that seriously: resentment, in his view, is nature's defence, a guardian of justice. But he noticed a subtlety. The resentful person, Smith wrote, wants not so much to cause the offender pain as for the offender to realize that they are suffering precisely for what they did. That is, at the heart of revenge lies a thirst for acknowledgment — “let them understand they were wrong.” Smith added that the impartial spectator can share our resentment only when it is proportionate. So you needn't suppress this feeling; listen to it: what exactly needs to be acknowledged? Often the answer points to a path where no one is harmed — speaking up, holding a boundary, seeking justice.
revenge.practice: Say it aloud, in an empty room or on a walk: “What I want most is for this person to understand that…” — and finish the sentence. What of it can you acknowledge yourself, without waiting for them?

quote.text: Resentment seems to have been given us by nature for defence, and for defence only.
quote.author: Adam Smith
quote.source: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part II, Sec. II, Ch. 1

anger_at_loved.text: Adam Smith lived nearly all his life with his mother, and his remark on flare-ups at home is down-to-earth. Anger at those close to you is especially painful: shame follows, because you love them. He noticed that among strangers we instinctively pull ourselves together — we imagine how we look in their eyes and restrain our feelings. Among those close to us this inner spectator relaxes: we expect complete understanding from them and control ourselves less. Hence the paradox: the people dearest to us get the most of our outbursts. Anger at someone close is not a sign that love is absent but a sign of closeness and tiredness at once. Smith advised bringing back the outside view in difficult moments. This doesn't mean keeping your distance — only seeing the scene for a second through the eyes of a respectful guest before saying something you'll regret.
anger_at_loved.practice: For five seconds, imagine a guest you respect sitting in the room — Smith's “stranger.” Say what you wanted to say the way you would in front of them.

ambivalence.text: Hume looked at the soul almost like a chemist: what happens when two opposite passions are directed at the same object? When you love someone and can't stand them at once, it feels as if something is wrong with you — Hume didn't think so. Sometimes, he wrote, they alternate; sometimes they mix, the way liquids mix, and then a new, complex feeling results. For Hume, love and dislike are “indirect passions”: they are aroused by different qualities of a person, not by the person as a whole. Someone close can be warm and harsh, generous and unbearable at the same time — and your feelings are simply responding honestly to all of it at once. Ambivalence, then, is not confusion but accuracy. You don't have to pick one feeling as the “real” one: both tell the truth about different sides of the same relationship.
ambivalence.practice: Pour a glass of water and add a little juice or milk — watch the two liquids blend into a new color. That, for Hume, is how love and dislike mix; don't choose which one is “right.”

guilty_relief.text: Hume noticed that a single event almost always stirs several passions at once, simply because we look at it from different sides. Relief after a breakup, a departure, or even the death of a seriously ill loved one can be frightening: am I actually glad? The loss brings grief, and the end of long strain brings relief; these feelings don't cancel each other out, they simply belong to different facets of the same thing. Adam Smith would suggest imagining an impartial spectator who knows everything: how much you bore, how many nights you didn't sleep, how long you were afraid. Such a witness would not condemn you. They would understand that relief is the natural response of body and soul to a weight finally lifted. And that love hasn't gone anywhere.
guilty_relief.practice: Put one palm on your chest and the other on your belly: let one hold the grief, the other the relief. Breathe like this for a minute without letting go of either.

indifference.text: “They appear so cold, and strained, and ridiculous,” Hume admitted of his own recent passions of the mind. Sometimes an event “should” move you, yet inside it's quiet — and that's unsettling: am I callous? Hume explained that our sympathy — the capacity to catch others' feelings — depends on closeness: we respond more strongly to what is near, similar and vivid. When something is far away, abstract or simply too enormous, the imagination can't cope and the feeling doesn't arise. This is not a vice but how human nature works. Hume also distinguished the “calm passions”: they don't stir us violently, so they're easy to mistake for an absence of feeling, even though they can shape our actions. Indifference is sometimes not emptiness but a calm feeling that hasn't yet taken shape, or a tiredness of sympathy. You can give it time without pretending.
indifference.practice: Sit in silence for five minutes and ask yourself: if a feeling were there after all, only very quiet, what would it be? Listen for it as for a “calm passion,” and name one word, even if you're unsure.

escape.text: In 1734 Hume took a post with a Bristol sugar merchant, soon realized it wasn't for him, and within months left for France to write his Treatise. He knew firsthand the urge to quit a job, a city or a role and leave: it signals that life has grown too tight. Adam Smith, for his part, warned against the opposite: he described a man who toils all his life for rank and wealth and at the end notices that he has been chasing “trinkets.” Together, the two views give you a good question: what am I running from, and what do I want to reach? Sometimes the urge to escape points to a real need for change, sometimes to tiredness that needs rest. The feeling itself doesn't commit you to any decision, but it deserves to be heard.
escape.practice: Take a walk, like Hume on the roads of France, if only to the end of the street and back: on the way out, think about what you want to leave; on the way back, about what you want to reach.

forbidden_attraction.text: Hume watched the passions like a naturalist watching weather — without preaching. An attraction to someone unavailable or “wrong” is unsettling, especially if you never meant to feel it; Hume helps you look at it calmly. He held that the passions don't obey reason's commands: reason can suggest how to act, but it cannot simply cancel a feeling. And in the Treatise he noted that obstacles and uncertainty usually strengthen a passion rather than weaken it: whatever is hard to attain, the imagination paints especially vividly. Part of the force of such an attraction lies in its very unavailability. This is not a verdict on the feeling, nor advice about what to do with it. It simply lifts the shame: you're not a “bad person,” you're a person with an imagination. It can help to ask what exactly in this image is so alluring.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Run a Humean experiment in your imagination: suppose the obstacles vanished and this person were free and available. What happened to the pull — did it grow, stay, or fade?

social_anxiety.text: Lost in thought, Adam Smith once wandered miles from home in his dressing gown — and the world survived. Fear of judgment turns conversations into trials, and Smith knew where it comes from. Adam Smith wrote that from childhood we learn to see ourselves through others' eyes — society is like a mirror to us. Hence our sensitivity to how we're seen. But Smith also made an observation that is reassuring. The spectator, he held, always feels another's state far more faintly than the one living it: it takes an effort of imagination, and their attention is occupied by their own life. So others notice our awkwardness far less than it seems to us. Besides, Smith set against the real spectators “the man within the breast” — the inner impartial spectator. Its judgment matters more than the crowd's approval, and it is usually kinder to your nervousness than you are.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a conversation, pick one question you genuinely want to ask — after all, Smith's “spectator” is busy with their own life too. Ask it and listen to the answer.

uncertainty.text: Hume compared the soul to a stringed instrument: after each stroke the strings keep sounding, and before one feeling has died away, another rushes in. Uncertainty exhausts you in just this way — it's hard to plan and hard to settle down. When the outcome is unknown, the imagination darts between the good possibility and the bad one, and out of this wavering hope and fear are born — a mixture of joy and sorrow. This explains why uncertainty is so tiring — the problem isn't weakness but constant swaying. Hume, though, offered something to hold on to: believe in proportion to the evidence. No more and no less than the facts suggest. This lets you avoid inventing the worst outcome as if it had already happened, and avoid demanding a certainty from yourself that isn't available yet.
uncertainty.practice: Press your palm flat on the table, the way a musician damps a string, and hold it for three slow breaths. Then say aloud what you know for sure and what you only suppose.

quote.text: A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.
quote.author: David Hume
quote.source: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. X

waiting.text: Twice Hume waited in vain for a professorship, yet he lived those years fully — writing, arguing, dining with friends. Waiting for an answer, results or news makes time viscous, and your thoughts keep circling back. Hume noticed that the imagination paints events near in time especially vividly: the closer the hour, the brighter the picture and the stronger the agitation. That is why waiting is so consuming. In his essay “Of Refinement in the Arts,” Hume wrote that human happiness consists of three ingredients: action, pleasure and repose. Waiting is agonizing also because it crowds out all three: we don't act, don't enjoy, don't rest — we just hang there. What can help is not the effort to “stop thinking” but a small return of at least one of these three things. The waiting won't vanish, but it will stop filling the day.
waiting.practice: For the next hour, choose one of Hume's three threads of happiness — a small task, a small pleasure or real rest — and give it room beside the waiting.

regret.text: “The great source of both the misery and disorders of human life seems to arise from over-rating the difference between one permanent situation and another,” Adam Smith wrote. Regret over something done or left undone can be very stubborn, behind it lies care for your own life, and Smith's line applies to it directly. We imagine that on the other road everything would have been completely different, and this picture is brighter than reality because it can never be tested. Part of the pain of regret is that the missed option seems perfect. Smith added something else: a fair inner spectator judges us by what we knew and could do at the time, not by what became known later. You can keep regret as a lesson, but not as a verdict on your former self.
regret.practice: Imagine the “other road” not as perfect but as ordinary — with its own difficulties, boredom and losses. Live in it honestly for a minute, like Smith's spectator, then come back here.

quote.text: The great source of both the misery and disorders of human life, seems to arise from over-rating the difference between one permanent situation and another.
quote.author: Adam Smith
quote.source: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part III, Ch. 3

longing.text: The picture of an absent friend, Hume noted, instantly enlivens our idea of him: resemblance draws the image after it, and the image draws feeling. Missing someone makes their presence almost tangible — precisely because they aren't here. Our ideas are connected with one another by three principles: resemblance, contiguity in time and place, and cause and effect. So everything reminds you of the person: a similar voice, a place you used to go together, a habit they left in you. Your mind isn't to blame for returning to them again and again — that is how association works. Longing is not a failing but the trace someone dear has left in the very fabric of your thoughts. It doesn't need to be driven out. You can notice which things stir it most, and allow yourself the sadness without being frightened by how often it comes.
longing.practice: Hold an object or photo connected with this person and let Humean association do its work: just look for a minute and notice which warm memory arrives first.

world_pain.text: Hume considered sympathy — the capacity to catch the feelings of others — the most remarkable quality of human nature, and saw in it the basis of morality. Pain for the world — grim news, injustice, others' grief — is a sign of that living response, even when it weighs on you as though you had to carry it alone. But Adam Smith made a sober observation. He wrote that we cannot feel distant misfortunes as keenly as our own, and he argued with the moralists who reproach people for being able to rejoice while others somewhere are suffering. Such artificial compassion, in his view, helps no one. Smith advised not forcing yourself to grieve endlessly, but keeping your sensitivity alive and doing what is truly within your power. So protecting your ability to feel joy is not indifference but a condition for keeping compassion from burning out.
world_pain.practice: Do one small thing within your reach — for someone nearby or for people far away — and then one thing for yourself: tea, a walk, music. Smith held that joy doesn't betray compassion.

rejection.text: “Man naturally desires, not only to be loved, but to be lovely” — with this line Adam Smith opens a chapter of his book. That is why rejection hurts so: the wish to be accepted runs deep in us. Hume helps you see a trap the mind often falls into after a refusal. He described the “general rules” the imagination builds too hastily: it turns a single case into a law and extends it to everything similar. That is how one refusal quickly swells into the conclusion “no one will ever accept me.” The pain of rejection is real, but its generalization is the work of the imagination, not a proven fact. Hume suggested correcting hasty rules by attending to the evidence: how many times have you actually been accepted, valued, chosen? One refusal speaks of a meeting between two people, not of your worth.
rejection.practice: Test the Humean “general rule”: recall three times you were accepted, listened to or invited — and set them on the scale beside the one refusal.

abandonment.text: One billiard ball strikes another, and we expect the second to roll — Hume showed that this expectation rests on custom, not proof. The fear of being abandoned is born the same way: it can live for years and flare up at small things — a delayed reply, a cool tone of voice. We expect the future to resemble the past not because this has been proven but by “custom”: if something has happened repeatedly, the mind reaches for the same conclusion by itself. If you were left in the past, the imagination will keep painting the same ending. This doesn't mean you exaggerate on purpose: that is how habit works, and the old experience was real. But Hume also showed that habit is not prophecy. New repetitions gradually create a new habit. So it's worth noticing each time someone close to you stays — this slowly retrains the expectation.
abandonment.practice: Start a Humean “log of experience”: a short list of times people stayed or came back. Add even small things — custom is retrained by repetition.

unrequited.text: Hume unravelled the amorous passion into three threads: delight in beauty, bodily appetite and generous goodwill. Unrequited love is one of the loneliest pains: the feeling is there, but no answer comes. Adam Smith noticed, with unexpected honesty, that to an outsider its intensity always seems out of proportion, since they don't see what the lover sees. So even friends may find it hard to grasp the depth of what you're going through, and that loneliness is not your fault. Hume, for his part, linked love with the wish for the other's good. Your love is neither a mistake nor a humiliation: it speaks of your ability to see something beautiful in another person. Hume also noticed that feelings not fed by new impressions gradually grow calmer. This won't happen on command, but it will happen — and your capacity to love will stay with you.
unrequited.practice: Hume linked love with wishing the other well. Do one kind thing today for someone else entirely — a neighbor, a friend, a stranger — and notice that your capacity to love hasn't gone anywhere.

humiliation.text: Hume, famous and very stout, once got stuck in a bog below Edinburgh Castle; a passing fishwife would pull the “atheist” out only if he recited the Lord's Prayer — and he did. Humiliation wounds because it strikes at your dignity. Adam Smith understood this: he wrote that an undeserved reproach can painfully wound even very steadfast people. But he also offered something to lean on. Smith distinguished two tribunals: “the man without” — real witnesses — and “the man within the breast,” the impartial spectator who knows all the circumstances and your intentions. Humiliation is the verdict of the outer tribunal, often unjust, passed in haste or malice. The inner tribunal can review it. Being treated humiliatingly says something about the situation and about those who acted like that, but it does not determine your worth. It still hurts; what matters is whose voice has the last word.
humiliation.practice: Like someone just out of a bog, brush yourself off — literally, palms over shoulders and sleeves — and stand up straight. Tell yourself: “The outer court passed a sentence; the inner one hasn't signed it.”

body_shame.text: “A turtle-eating alderman rather than a refined philosopher” — so one aristocrat described the stout Hume, whom the Paris salons nonetheless adored. Dissatisfaction with your body rarely comes from nowhere: from childhood we are judged and compared. In the Treatise, Hume noted that the beauty or deformity of the body, like our other qualities, affects pride and humility largely through the imagined gaze of others. And in his essay “Of the Standard of Taste” he wrote a sentence that changes a lot: beauty is not a quality of things themselves; it exists in the mind of the one who looks, and different minds perceive different beauty. So a judgment about your body is a judgment of someone's taste — often borrowed from the era — and not an objective fact. This won't make you love yourself in a minute, but it weakens the power of a single “correct” ideal.
body_shame.practice: Hume valued the body for the living impressions it gives. Name one impression your body gave you today — the taste of tea, the sun's warmth, your steps — and silently thank it.

quote.text: Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them; and each mind perceives a different beauty.
quote.author: David Hume

illness.text: As a young man Hume struggled for several years with an ailment that neither doctors nor friends really understood. When the body lets you down, there's not only pain but loneliness, and Adam Smith explained why. He wrote that others share bodily pain only very faintly: it's hard for the imagination to reproduce a sensation that isn't in one's own body. So people's sympathy often seems insufficient — and the problem is not that they don't believe you but the limits of human sympathy. Knowing this can ease some of the hurt, both toward them and toward yourself for “complaining too much.” Hume added that even in hard times the soul holds on to small habits, company and simple pleasures. So you needn't demand heroism of yourself; you can take care of the little that brings warmth right now.
illness.practice: Tell one close person about a single concrete sensation of today — not “I feel bad,” but “my knees ache and it's hard to focus.” Smith would say concreteness helps another's imagination reach you.

pride.text: “Love of literary fame, my ruling passion,” Hume wrote without embarrassment in his short autobiography. Pride in what you've done is a good, well-earned feeling, and there's no need to hide it. Hume treated it with respect: in the Treatise he called pride an agreeable passion that arises when something valuable is connected with ourselves — our work, a skill, an action. He distinguished conceit, which irritates others, from a well-founded sense of one's own worth, and considered the latter necessary for life: it gives us confidence in our undertakings. Adam Smith added that the best pride is the kind an impartial spectator would approve — that is, deserved. If you feel it now, you needn't hurry to rein yourself in. Look at what exactly you did, and allow yourself to acknowledge it.
pride.practice: Tell one person what exactly you did and what quality of yours it showed — so that Smith's impartial spectator would nod: deserved.

quote.text: Nothing is more useful to us in the conduct of life, than a due degree of pride, which makes us sensible of our own merit, and gives us a confidence and assurance in all our projects and enterprizes.
quote.author: David Hume
quote.source: A Treatise of Human Nature, Book III, Part 3, Sec. 2

melancholy.text: Why do audiences gladly go to the theatre to weep at a tragedy and leave satisfied? Hume devoted his essay “Of Tragedy” to this riddle — and it bears directly on gentle melancholy, a quiet state in which sadness is somehow pleasant. His answer: when sorrow is clothed in beautiful form — in words, music, images — the very stirring of sorrow merges with the pleasure of beauty, and the feeling becomes different, soft and full. Melancholy, then, is sadness that has managed to find a form. It doesn't need to be cured or hurriedly dispelled. Hume, who loved both solitary reflection and the company of friends, would more likely advise you to stay in it for a while and then return to people. Melancholy may turn out to be a time when you hear yourself best.
melancholy.practice: Give the sadness Hume's “beautiful form”: play one song or read aloud one poem that matches it, and stay with it to the end.
